STATEMENTS
Death Penalty

Mr DREYFUS (Isaacs) (09:01): by leave—Australia opposes the death penalty in all circumstances for all people. This is not the position of one government or one party; it is a longstanding bipartisan commitment grounded in our belief in the inherent rights and dignity of every person. When serious crimes occur, the grief and anger are real, and the desire for justice is entirely human.

But when we look at how the death penalty is used around the world, it becomes clear that it does not deliver justice; it is an affront to it. First, the evidence shows that the death penalty is too often applied unfairly to people facing economic or educational disadvantage; people living with intellectual, cognitive and psychosocial disability; foreign nationals; women; and ethnic minorities. Second, when mistakes are made—and they are—there is no undoing them; there is no second chance. Third, the death penalty offers no prospect of rehabilitation. Fourth, the death penalty does not make communities safer; there is no evidence that it deters crime more effectively than other serious penalties. Finally, in some countries, people can still be put to death for who they love, for what they believe or as a form of political persecution. That is not justice.

Australia works for global abolition through every channel available multilaterally, regionally and bilaterally. We use international forums, particularly the UN, to call for universal abolition. We raise our position directly with retentionist countries, including our close partners. These conversations are often private, but they matter. And we do this work alongside civil society, whose efforts are vital.

Australia's own journey is one we can be proud of. Our last execution, of Ronald Ryan, took place in 1967; the 60th anniversary of this event is coming up next year. The death penalty was abolished across every Australian jurisdiction in 1985, and in 2010 parliament legislated to ensure it can never return. In 2018 we launched our first strategy for the global abolition of the death penalty under then Foreign minister Bishop. In 2022 we co-led the UN General Assembly resolution on the death penalty, and a record number of nations voted in favour.

Last year, the Prime Minister and the Foreign minister asked me, as Special Envoy for International Human Rights, to take on a special advocacy role for universal abolition. Today I'm proud to announce another milestone, the launch of Australia's refreshed strategy for abolition of the death penalty. Under this refreshed strategy, Australia will broaden and strengthen our abolition efforts. This will include deepening our engagement with civil society, countering the disproportionate and discriminatory application of the death penalty on certain individuals, combating efforts to subvert international human rights obligations and ensuring abolition is a whole-of-government effort. The refreshed strategy is closely informed by the recommendations of the Human Rights Subcommittee of the Joint Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs and Trade, which the government welcomed earlier this year. This occasion is an opportunity to reflect on global progress. There are 146 countries which have now abolished the death penalty in law or in practice. Lebanon abolished it this year, becoming the first country in the Middle East to do so. I was honoured to personally congratulate Lebanon's ambassador to Australia a few weeks ago. Vietnam has reduced the number of offences carrying the death penalty, and Zimbabwe has abolished it for ordinary crimes. In 2023, Malaysia abolished the mandatory death penalty, and Pakistan repealed it for drug related offences.

In these times, when so many hard won gains are being tested, we must guard against backsliding. Progress is not inevitable. Amnesty International reports that executions worldwide in 2025 were the highest since 1981, a 78 per cent increase on 2024. Drug related offences accounted for at least 46 per cent of them. Our home, the Asia-Pacific, remains the region with the most executions. Given this, Australia's leadership remains crucial. Today I remember those who have been put to death, including Australians. I also think of those who remain on death row worldwide. I recognise the tireless advocates, lawyers, parliamentarians and civil-society organisations who refuse to look away. Abolition has been achieved by countries in every region of the world, across different cultures, traditions, religions and legal systems. It is not the project of one group of states. It is a global movement rooted in the protection of human rights, so I repeat: Australia opposes the death penalty in all circumstances for all people. Under our refreshed strategy, we will continue working until universal abolition is achieved. I ask leave of the House to present a copy of Australia's strategy for global abolition of the death penalty 2026.
Leave granted.
Mr TED O'BRIEN (Fairfax) (09:08): by leave—In his recent encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas, published in May this year, Pope Leo XIV wrote:
No sin, failure, humiliation or exclusion can diminish the profound value of a human life …

I reflect on these words as I rise to acknowledge the government's tabling of Australia's strategy for global abolition of the death penalty 2026. I oppose the death penalty, and while I open with the words of Pope Leo, my opposition is driven not by my religion but by my conscience. Indeed, allow me to quote from another great theologian, John Henry Newman, who famously declared, as if he were proposing a toast:
I shall drink to the Pope, if you please, still, to conscience first, and to the Pope afterwards.

When the former coalition government launched Australia's strategy for the abolition of the death penalty in 2018, it outlined four compelling reasons for opposing capital punishment. First, the death penalty is irrevocable. When justice fails and an innocent person has been executed, there can be no remedy. Second, it denies any opportunity for rehabilitation, redemption or reform. Third, there is no convincing evidence that the death penalty deters crime more effectively than life imprisonment. And, fourth, it is disproportionately imposed upon society's most vulnerable, including the poor, minorities and those least able to defend themselves.

These were compelling arguments in 2018, and they are compelling still today. I acknowledge that the government's updated strategy reaffirms these principles, but, personally and guided by conscience, I believe there is a fifth. Although in order of importance, I put this one first, right at the top. That is that the death penalty is inherently inhumane. It violates the sanctity of life and the fundamental dignity of the individual. This is not to diminish the gravity of heinous crimes nor the suffering of the victims and their families. Justice must be served. The gravest crimes demand the most severe penalties. The rights of victims must be honoured, and society must be protected, but we can condemn the crime, punish the offender and uphold justice without resorting to taking a human life. Human dignity is not something bestowed by governments. It is not something earned through good behaviour. It is not something forfeited through wrongdoing. I believe no state should possess the power to extinguish it.

My office received the government's strategy only last evening, affording me limited time this morning—indeed, little more than the past hour—to take a quick read and formulate my remarks this morning in response to the tabling of the report by the special envoy. My colleagues and I will therefore examine the strategy in detail before offering a formal response on behalf of the coalition, but I want to take this opportunity to acknowledge the tireless work of those who have championed this cause over many years, in particular the Parliamentary Friends of Global Abolition of the Death Penalty, co-chaired by the envoy and Senator Dean Smith. I also want to acknowledge the fine work of the Joint Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade, particularly their Human Rights subcommittee, which tabled a comprehensive report in December 2024 on its inquiry into Australia's efforts to advocate for the worldwide abolition of the death penalty. Their work reminds us that some causes are greater than partisan politics.

Each of us is privileged to serve in parliament, and we carry a responsibility to uphold and promote the values that define Australia as one of the world's greatest liberal democracies—values of freedom, equality and a fair go. I have long argued that a nation's foreign policy is an outward expression of its values and interests, and, if we believe in the sanctity of human life and if we believe in the dignity of the individual, then those convictions must find expression in our dealings with the world. That is why advocating for the global abolition of the death penalty must remain a core tenet of Australian foreign policy, not because we seek to lecture others but because we have a responsibility to stand for what we believe is right and because the universal dignity of human life knows no national borders.
Justice must always be pursued, but justice must never come at the expense of our humanity. That is the principle I stand for, and it is the principle Australia must continue to advocate for.

Consideration resumed of the motion:

to which the following amendment was moved:
That all words after "That" be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:
"whilst not declining to give the bill a second reading, the House:
(1) notes that:
(a) the Government did not take a minimum tax on discretionary trusts to the 2025 election and promised before that election not to raise taxes;

(b) Treasury's own Impact Analysis says around 350,000 small businesses operate through a discretionary trust, and that each of them is left with three options: pay a new 30 per cent tax, restructure and pay stamp duty, or lock in fixed shares for life in a one-off election in 2028-29;
(c) Treasury puts the compliance cost at an average of $141.5 million per year;
(d) twelve matters are left to legislative instruments that have not been released, and consultation ran for less than the 30-day minimum set by the Government's own Office of Impact Analysis; and
(2) calls on the Government to:
(a) withdraw the minimum tax on discretionary trusts, or, failing that, delay the start of the minimum tax on discretionary trusts by 12 months, to 1 July 2029; and
(b) split the bill such that the capital gains tax amendments, the definition of a new residential dwelling and the payday superannuation transitional relief can be dealt with separately".
to which the following amendment was moved:
That all words after "notes that" be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:
"(a) the bill intends to exclude genuine testamentary trusts from the minimum tax on discretionary trusts;

(b) the bill applies a beneficiary test to testamentary trusts 'established' on or after 1 July 2028, but does not say whether a testamentary trust is established when the will is made, when the will-maker dies, or when estate assets pass to the trustee;
(c) as a result, Australians making or reviewing a will cannot know whether the trust it creates will be covered by the new rules; and
(2) calls on the Government to amend the bill so that:

(a) the beneficiary test applies only where a testamentary trust is established under will or codicil provisions made or varied on or after 1 July 2028, under a court order made on or after that date, or on an intestacy where the deceased died on or after that date; and

(b) the exclusion applies to income derived for the benefit of an individual, an exempt entity or the trustee of a special disability trust, so that naming an ineligible beneficiary in a will does not affect the treatment of the trust's other income".
to which the following amendment was moved:
That the following words be added after paragraph (2):
"(3) further notes that:
(a) small and family businesses are the backbone of the Australian economy, supporting employment, investment, innovation and local communities;
(b) small businesses face growing cost pressures from the cumulative impact of taxation, reporting and regulation across government portfolios;

(c) government policy decisions, like the proposed 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts, are too often assessed individually, without adequately considering their cumulative impact on small businesses; and
(d) the existing Impact Analysis Framework does not require dedicated, independent Small Business Impact Statements for all major policy decisions across portfolios; and
(4) calls on the Government to:

(a) mandate publicly available Small Business Impact Statements for all major policy decisions materially affecting small businesses, prepared or independently assessed by a strengthened and adequately resourced Office of Impact Analysis; and
(b) require ministers to publicly explain how small business impacts have been addressed and what measures have been taken to minimise regulatory and compliance burdens".

Mr TIM WILSON (Goldstein) (09:48): The idea that this Albanese government would continue to increase costs to small business at a time when they are desperate and begging for relief—the only answer from this Albanese government is to turn around and impose higher taxes on them. We believe that there should be a splitting of this bill because we believe that measures that are necessary to protect small business should be excluded. Instead, the government is only piling on the pressure and breaking small business. We only heard yesterday of new inflation data which outlined the higher pressures and higher costs that are going to be imposed on small businesses. The solution from this government is to turn around and say: 'It's fine. We're going to impose higher taxes, higher costs, $50,000 per Australian small business, to navigate and steer through the higher costs being imposed by this legislation.' We're not just hearing that; we're hearing about a $13.3 billion deadweight cost to the entirety of the Australian economy. What is it that this government doesn't get? What don't they understand about the laws they're introducing? Why don't they understand they're breaking families, breaking small businesses and breaking people's hopes, dreams and livelihoods? Hundreds of thousands of small businesses across this country are being targeted and attacked, assaulted by the Albanese government, because it cannot control its spending addiction. As a consequence, they are being sent to the cleaners.

We know how bad things are now. It's only going to get worse, because every time inflation goes up, interest rates go up. We know next Tuesday, while many people are hoping for a win from the race that stops the nation, what they're going to be at risk of is further punishment by the Albanese government and its inflation addiction. We always come into this parliament and talk about the problems of addiction. We always come in and say, 'We've got to support people through their pain and make sure they're not exposed.' When is this Treasurer going to have his spending addiction brought under control? When are we going to see legislation from the other side of the chamber saying that we've got to control this Treasurer and his spending addiction because he is sending Australian families backwards?

If it was a gambling company, they'd be straight on their feet and acting. Even worse than that, they'd turn around and make sure that there was intervention and action every step of the way. But we don't see similar action when it's their own, because, at the end of the day, in their lust for power, the Labor Party will focus on one thing, which is: how can they feed themselves at the expense of the Australian people? They're turning around to the small businesses of the nation, who are already struggling to keep their doors open, already struggling to pay their costs, already struggling to pay their tax bills, struggling to pay the tens of thousands of dollars of surcharge fees, struggling to meet their basic needs so they can pay their staff before they even give a second to thinking about paying themselves. And what's the answer from this government? What's the answer from this Treasurer? It's to impose higher costs so the government can pay themselves first.

We do not believe in that vision or that future for this country—sorry! We do not believe the strength of Australia is built from a government that cannot control its spending addiction. We believe in a nation where we back families, communities and small businesses as the foundation of this nation's success. We are completely unapologetic about splitting this bill so that we can make sure we protect Australian families, small businesses and households. We have no apology for standing up against this Treasurer and his inflation addiction, because if we don't stand up, then no-one will.

We've seen too many times—we just saw in the chamber then—Teal MPs once again betraying their constituents, as they're so wont to do, by voting for a minimum tax on small business. You look at it and think, 'What is wrong with these MPs?' They do not understand the consequences. Neither do members of the Labor Party. I can assure members opposite, on the other side, that they might carry on with their hubris and, lemming-like, follow this Prime Minister and this Treasurer off the political cliff, but the small businesses of this nation will remember at the next election what you did. They will be able to say, 'We know what you did in the last parliamentary term.' They will look at you and say: 'You betrayed the Australian people. You betrayed Australian small businesses. You betrayed the families that depend on them. You betrayed the employees that depend on them.' And for what purpose? So that you can rapaciously satisfy the needs and the spending addiction of the Prime Minister and the Treasurer.
The game is up. We're going to fight and we're going to fight all the way to the next election.

Ms CHANEY (Curtin) (10:00): I support the intent of this bill, which is to tax income in a broadly similar way whether it comes from work or from wealth, and I welcome the changes the government has made following consultation, including the electable regime and rollover relief. But we're asking family businesses to make significant decisions quickly without knowing what those decisions will cost—Treasury puts the average cost of restructuring at around $11,000; COSBOA puts it at $15,000 to $50,000 before stamp duty—and the window for making a decision closes early, with rollover relief ending on 30 June 2030.

My amendments would make sure we find out how this reform is affecting small business while there's still time to fix any problems. These amendments insert a new schedule, 3A, which sets up two reviews. The first is an early inquiry by the Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman. The minister would ask the ombudsman by 1 July 2029 to inquire into how the trust changes are affecting small business, using the ombudsman's existing inquiry powers. The ombudsman would report by 31 March 2030, three months before rollover relief closes, and the report would be tabled in parliament. The ombudsman would look at how small businesses are using rollover relief and the option to fix beneficiaries and stay outside the minimum tax and whether those settings, including the June 2030 end date, should change. It would look at what businesses are really paying to adjust, including professional fees and state stamp duty, it would look at whether ATO guidance and support are adequate, and it would look for any unintended consequences. The amendment also lets the ombudsman request aggregate data from the Commissioner of Taxation on rollovers and elections. No individual or business would be identified, but it would give the ombudsman hard data to consider alongside what small businesses are saying. The timing of this review is important. If costs turn out much higher than expected or ATO guidance arrives late, we need to know before the deadline for rollover relief passes, not after businesses have made decisions that they can't undo. A report in March 2030 gives the parliament time to extend the deadline if it needs to do so.

The second review is a full, independent review of the trust amendments. At the moment, the bill requires no review at all, which is a significant gap for a reform that impacts 840,000 discretionary trusts. This amendment would require an independent review to begin between July 2030 and January 2031, once there's tax data to show how the new rules are working in practice. It must be conducted by people who are not officials of Treasury or the ATO, completed within nine months and tabled within 15 sitting days. The review would go back to the purpose of the bill and ask: has it brought the taxation of trust income closer to the taxation of income from work? It would compare actual revenue and compliance costs with the published estimates and identify which income and wealth groups have ended up paying more. On small business, it would look at how much additional tax has been paid, what restructuring really costs and the effect on investment and succession planning. It would examine how people have changed their structures, including any shift towards companies, and it would examine how the commissioner and the minister have used their discretionary powers under the rollover and election regimes—because powers of this kind should be open to scrutiny.

These amendments don't change the tax, and they don't cost the budget. They simply make sure parliament sees the real-world impact of this reform, not just the modelling, and has the chance to respond. Getting the detail right is how this reform can keep the community's support. I call on the government to support these amendments and commit to these reviews. I commend the amendments to the House.

Mr JOYCE (New England) (11:05): I just want to run you through some certain issues. This is obviously about getting access to some of your super, and it's not all your super. It's a portion of your super for a portion of time, because we firmly believe in One Nation that your super is not a national asset, it's your asset. One of the classic examples of where we've seen the government bereft of control over people's private assets would be in the Shield and First Guardian issue. I bring this up as an example because quite often I see the Assistant Treasurer going to the dispatch box talking about the sanctity of super, and what they've missed is that $1.2 billion was stolen from super. People were left with no money.

I want to give you an example of one. There's a company called Sequoia. It owns InterPrac, which is a licensed adviser for First Guardian and Shield. Now, here's an example of what has happened under this government's watch. There's a gentleman, Mr Richard Orr. He's 53 years old. He's terminally ill with cancer. He most likely won't make it till February. Instead of accessing his super to make his final memories with his wife and children, he is forced to battle Sequoia and InterPrac to have any of his super returned. Sequoia had sold InterPrac a fortnight ago to their former CEO who registered a new company, Bellbird, just one day prior to the sale. The sale means Sequoia's parent company of InterPrac are no longer liable for debts owed to victims like Mr Richard Orr, who is terminally ill with cancer. Investors like Melinda Kee are left to fight this injustice while these companies make a mockery of our government and the financial industry. These people have no money. They are broke. If the Labor Party believes in super so much, why don't you give these people who have been nurses and who have been teachers back the money that was stolen from them? They do not have the resources to pursue these people. They're making it so hard for Mr Orr to even get access to the court, just playing the game till Mr Orr dies.

That is why One Nation says this is your personal asset, a personal asset that must be protected, and an expression of a personal asset is your capacity to have access to it when you need it, when you're under the pump, when it looks like you might lose your house or be kicked out into the street because you can't pay your rent—a portion of it for a portion of time. Now, if you believe absolutely philosophically that this should never happen, well, you already allow it to happen. You already allow it to happen under items of distress. In fact, record numbers under this current economic environment are getting access to it, but it's so convoluted and it's so restricted.

There is an implication that it's the government's asset, the national asset. The great fear that so many people have as the government gets further and further and further into debt is that they'll look for a way to try and pay the debt off. And there's this big cherry sitting out there, $4.5 trillion in super. To pay off their trillion dollars in debt, they'll start reaching into the super. And you might say, 'That's paranoid.' No, it's not. They've already started. They've already started the legislation to get access to your super, changing the tax rates, changing the capacity for you to get [inaudible]. They changed it for people over $3 million, and they changed it for another level for people over 10. And you say, 'That's just the edge.'

So what we are doing here in this amendment is reinforcing our belief that super is actually an asset of the individual. It comes from their money that they earned. It's not from the taxpayer. If the government believe their protection of super and how they look after it is so paramount and that you should never get it out, then I challenge them to go to those people who were in First Guardian and Shield who still have not got a cent from the government, have not been paid out, are still bereft and are going to go into their retirement after being a teacher or a nurse their whole lives without a cent. Somebody in this building has got to stand up for these people. I intend to do that. I intend to do it deliberately. I intend to do it consistently. This is yet another example of reinvesting in the individual. It's their asset. If the government believes that they've got the greater protection on it, then it should go out and protect those people.

Ms SPENDER (Wentworth) (11:20): I support the government's intent to rebalance Australia's income tax system. Making our tax system fairer and more sustainable is long overdue, though I will continue to argue that you're not rebalancing the tax system and until you commit to giving back every tax dollar you raise to income tax cuts. Otherwise, you are just raising taxes. But rebalancing the system can't come at the expense of Australia's dynamism and capacity to innovate, and it shouldn't need to. That's why my amendment requires a review of the IBCC and of indexation model more broadly as it affects innovation and small business as soon as practicable after its first year of operation.

I acknowledge the government's efforts in designing the IBCC. Its purpose is to shield productive innovative businesses from an indexation system that could otherwise subject Australian founders, employees and investors to some of the highest taxes of capital in the world, but the concession is deliberately narrow, riddled with tripwires and adds complexity. I'd like to give you an example. Yesterday, I was contacted by the founder of a small, profitable Australian digital health company. It's about a decade old with customers here and overseas, and about 95 per cent of its profit comes back to Australia. The company has just won a contract with an American client that will make it double in size. To service it, the company needs operational staff on the ground in the US. The founder now believes he may fail the predominant activity test because slightly more than half his team could end up in the US, even though the profits still come home, so, instead of celebrating, he's talking to lawyers and accountants about restructuring so the business can stay in Australia and still qualify. He's wading through this legislation at the same time I am, trying to work out if the carve-out will protect his business.

This shows that the IBCC risks undermining its own aims. It's meant to support companies scaling here and internationally, yet one of its innovation principles requires to a company to show international competitiveness, while the predominant activity test requires half of its people to be in Australia. Succeed overseas and you risk losing the concession.

Good intentions are not enough. The design of the IBCC will have real, if unintended, consequences for Australian innovators. We need a system that is fair, simple and predictable. This is what encourages innovation and investment. The truth is the IBCC is just trying to patch a flawed system. The indexation on capital gains tax is just the wrong way to tax risk taking, especially in low-capital businesses. The combination of the IBCC and indexation has three major flaws. It is complex, which chases away capital and risk taking. It is unfair. It allows a government to determine which businesses are innovative and which businesses are not. As someone who has run businesses, I tell you every single business takes risk, takes guts and is bloody hard to do. Thirdly, it is uncompetitive. We are ending up in low-capital rates, in low-capital businesses, with people paying in the 40s potentially in capital gains tax. That is uncompetitive around the rest of the world, and we cannot pretend that won't have real impacts in this country.

I urge the government. There are better ways of doing this. I have put one forward myself. I don't know that it is perfect, but it is a darn sight better than what the government is proposing right now. The government should fix this because, whatever happens, believe me, this bill will come back one day, because the IBCC and the indexation of capital gains on risk taking just make no sense.

I also want to challenge the opposition on this. You have voted against this bill, and the IBCC is as flawed as it comes, but it is the one thing that might protect some tech companies staying in this country, so do not ignore this bill. I cannot see how you would vote against this bill, because it makes a difference to innovative businesses. I hate the bill. I hate the taxation of capital gains via indexation on risk taking, but the government and certainly the shadow Treasurer should know that, if you vote against the IBCC, technology businesses that are relying on this to try and help stay in this country really matter and will be hurt by it. And if you vote against the ESVCLP and VCLP changes in this bill, that will also hurt the venture sector, which we need to support right now, because the government has made a whole bunch of mistakes in this space.

I urge the government to accept this amendment. It is very reasonable. It is asking for a review after one year, because this legislation will affect productive businesses, and this is a real challenge to the economy, and I think it is one that absolutely needs to be dealt with.

Dr RYAN (Kooyong) (11:39): This amendment is modest, practical and reasonable. The bill removes supporting R&D activities from the R&D tax incentive. R&D activities are the supporting work that makes medical research, engineering and innovation possible. Since the exposure draft of this legislation was released, it's now been garnished with a new power allowing a minister to determine by legislative instrument which kinds of activities are integral to R&D under the R&D tax incentive. This legislative instrument is presumably the government's answer to the concerns raised in consultation regarding the removal of supporting R&D activities. The minister's determination will determine which activities stay inside the incentive and which fall out. It will shape how much support Australian businesses can receive for their research and development.

But under the bill, as it is currently drafted, before making that determination the Treasurer need consult only one person: the industry minister. The minister is not obliged to consult Industry Innovation and Science Australia, the expert board that this parliament established to actually decide what is and isn't research and development. The minister is not required to consult the tax office, which administers the offset and will have to apply whatever the minister determines. The businesses, the scientists, the medical researchers, the academics and the engineers who understand better than anyone in this place what research and development needs will not be consulted on those activities which are integral to their activities. A decision made that way risks picking winners and losers. The industries with the best access to ministers' offices may well see their sorts of activities recognised, but the small manufacturer in a regional town, the startup without a lobbyist and the researcher perhaps working in a hospital or in a university department who doesn't happen to know anyone in Canberra won't be represented, and they won't have a voice. Ms WATSON-BROWN (Ryan) (12:24): My amendments deal with some serious flaws in this bill. By setting up extensive new ministerial powers, including the power to exempt individual gas companies from regulations, this bill creates fertile ground for favours. Some would call it corruptibility. It would build a favour factory between gas companies and resource ministers: 'A few hundred thousand dollars in donations? Thank you very much. We'll put a carve-out in the regulation for you.' Specifically, this bill allows the minister to exempt gas corporations from the proposed domestic supply obligation. The entire purpose of this bill is to increase domestic gas supply, yet it gives the minister the power to exempt any company they like. We know that the gas companies are very generous donors to both sides of politics—and One Nation, too. They have covered all their bases, hedged their bets. This set-up means it doesn't matter if the government changes; decisions will always be made in the gas corporations' favour.

To dismantle this favour factory between the gas industry and political parties, my amendments prevent all political donations by the gas exporters regulated by this gas reserve legislation. My amendments also remove the open-ended ministerial discretion to create any circumstances in which a gas company meets its obligations to supply gas. We're deeply worried about this, because the minister can say to Santos, for example, 'If you promise to build a pipeline to open up Beetaloo Basin and release its 27 billion tonnes of emissions, we'll give you an exemption from the scheme for a few years.' In short, these powers, as they exist, can be used to encourage new gas development and create an incentive to open up new fields, even if they aren't economic.

I reject entirely the implication around corruptibility or other things she has put onto the record. The bill that is before parliament today is a landmark economic reform in the form of a domestic gas reservation. The simple matter is that this bill is about getting more Australian gas to Australian consumers and Australian industries. This is not a bill in regard to electoral reform or donations. That is an important matter, and it warrants careful consideration and proper scrutiny. Agreeing to these amendments would bypass the consultation, analysis and scrutiny that good lawmaking requires. Ms CHANEY (Curtin) (12:36): This is a modest amendment about the interaction between WA and this national domestic gas scheme. Technically, the domestic gas reservation would apply nationally, but the bill gives the minister the power to carve out facilities covered by an existing scheme. It's clear that the minister's intention is to carve out WA facilities, and I support this. WA has had its own domestic gas reservation policy since 2006, and it makes sense not to simply impose a second overlapping obligation on exporters operating under that scheme.

But the WA scheme has its problems. It generally requires LNG exporters to make the equivalent of 15 per cent of their gas exports available to the domestic market, but the obligation is measured over the life of the project rather than year by year. The terms are negotiated project by project and they're confidential, and there are questions about whether some exporters are delivering what Western Australia needs. The Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis estimates that WA gas producers supplied five to 10 per cent of their production to the domestic market between 2018 and 2024—clearly below the 15 per cent target. The DomGas Alliance, which represents major gas users, including Alcoa, Wesfarmers and Yara, says that since 2017 Woodside's Pluto LNG project has supplied just 3.7 per cent of the gas it's exported to the domestic market. If the Commonwealth is going to rely on the WA scheme as the reason for exempting exporters from the national scheme, we should have some confidence that the WA scheme will be honoured. That's the issue that my amendment addresses.

As the bill currently stands, the minister can reduce an exporter's federal obligation because an existing domestic gas reservation arrangement applies. The minister doesn't have to be satisfied that the exporter has arrangements in place to supply gas under the state scheme. That creates a fairly obvious gap. An exporter could receive relief from its federal obligation because the WA scheme exists without having arrangements in place to provide the gas that the WA scheme is supposed to secure. The exporter gets the benefit of the carve-out, but Western Australians may not get the gas. My amendment adds a simple safeguard; it keeps the government's existing test but requires that the minister be satisfied of one additional thing—that arrangements are in place for the exporter to supply or to arrange to supply gas to the domestic market in accordance with the reservation arrangements that apply to it. Importantly, this does not change the WA scheme. It doesn't remove the WA carve-out and it doesn't impose new obligations on WA exporters. It simply says that, if an exporter is going to receive the benefit of the carve-out, there should be arrangements in place to meet the WA scheme.

I acknowledge that this amendment doesn't solve every problem with the WA scheme; it only tests whether those arrangements are in place. It's a very low hurdle to meet, but that should make it easier to accept. This amendment will become more important as WA's gas market tightens. The Australian Energy Market Operator projects gaps in the WA market from 2030, with those gaps growing in the years that follow. Before projected shortages are used to make the case for new gas developments like Browse, with the significant climate pollution that that would bring, we should make sure exporters are delivering the gas they have already agreed to provide to Western Australians.

This is a modest amendment. If the WA scheme is the reason an exporter receives relief from the national obligation, the minister should at least be satisfied that the arrangements are in place to honour that scheme. I'd hope that this outcome would be supported by both sides of the House as well as the people and government of WA. It tells the gas exporters who are not delivering on their state based obligation that this isn't good enough. This is an improvement that delivers for Western Australians and Western Australia, and I commend the amendment to the House.

The domestic gas reservation scheme does apply nationally. Our constitution prevents, quite rightly, the Commonwealth from giving states and territories preferential treatment. This bill defines a domestic gas market as a market and a part of Australia where natural gas is acquired and supplied by means of a physical network of interconnected gas pipelines. Under the legislation, all LNG exporters will be required to hold an export licence regardless of their location.

In practice, as the member will know, the east and west coast markets are physically separate, certainly in terms of those interconnected pipelines, and conditions in one market do not necessarily reflect conditions in the other. The scheme has the flexibility to recognise this, and it is fit for purpose. The legislation does recognise existing reservation arrangements and allows for domestic supply obligations to be adjusted in appropriate circumstances to take into account demand and supply conditions in the market. Domestic supply obligations are linked to the domestic market from which the LNG is exported, meaning exporters continue to supply the market to which they are physically connected.

Western Australia introduced its gas reservation policy many years ago and has largely managed its supply well. I accept too that it has not been perfect, and I acknowledge the comments of others, especially those from Western Australia, about that. However, it does have a system, and it's different to the system we're proposing, with different means of addressing demand over time and their demand calibration. Whilst working not perfectly but largely well, it is wise to let that remain in place. For these reasons the government will not be supporting the amendment, but I thank you for your contribution.

Dr SCAMPS (Mackellar) (12:49): I rise to speak to my amendments to the Domestic Gas Reservation Bill 2026. These are relatively straightforward amendments that seek to improve the operation of the scheme and ensure it remains responsive to changing circumstances over time. The first amendment would limit LNG export licences to a maximum term of 10 years, rather than allowing licences to be issued for periods of 20 to 50 years. This amendment reflects recommendations from stakeholders including Climateworks and the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis. Australia's gas market will not look the same in 10, 20, 30 or 50 years as it does today. We know the LNG export sector is projected to decline over the coming decade, including under assumptions outlined in the government's Future Gas Strategy. Given the uncertainty, it makes sense to periodically reassess export licences rather than lock in arrangements for several decades at a time.

A 10-year licence period would reduce the risk of government needing to intervene to amend or revoke long-term licences as domestic gas market conditions, reserve estimates or emissions policies change. It would also allow consideration of the impact of proposed exports on Australia's emission reduction targets as circumstances and policy settings evolve. Importantly, it would provide a clear and predictable review process, allowing licences to expire and be reassessed rather than relying on governments having to intervene ad hoc if circumstances change significantly.

At the same time, the amendment would continue to provide certainty for industry and LNG export contracts. Most east coast LNG sale agreements are due to expire by 2036, and there are currently no new major LNG export projects under development. The amendment would also ensure there is an opportunity to periodically assess whether licence holders remain fit and proper entities to hold an export licence.

My second amendment would make clear that the reservation scheme should operate consistently with Australia's emission reduction commitments. Specifically, it would add an object to the act requiring that its objectives be achieved in a way that does not jeopardise Australia's greenhouse gas emission reduction targets. It would also require the minister and regulator to take all reasonable steps to ensure decisions made under the act do not undermine achievement of those targets. Decisions made under the gas reservation scheme should take into account Australia's existing emissions reduction commitments, and measures designed to improve domestic gas supply should not have unintended consequences for those objectives.
These amendments reflect recommendations made in the ongoing inquiry into this bill and would, in my view, strengthen the bill in a practical and sensible way. I commend the amendments to the House.

Ms MADELEINE KING (Brand—Minister for Resources and Minister for Northern Australia) (12:52): I thank the member for Mackellar for her engagement on this package of bills. We all want, and agree that there should be, an orderly and ambitious energy transition, and that's why the Albanese Labor government has legislated emission targets; reformed the Safeguard Mechanism; and published the Future Gas Strategy, which mapped out the role of Australian gas in the energy transition and, of course, the transition of our whole region and our regional trading partners. We have also invested heavily in electrifying homes and installing batteries, with record take-up right around the country, and we've invested in building renewables at record rates.

The Domestic Gas Reservation Scheme will ensure that Australians can still access affordable gas while they still need it. Five million homes in this country still rely on gas for heating; that's especially the case in Victoria and here in the Australian Capital Territory. They also rely on gas for cooking and hot water. Cheaper gas prices will help some industries decarbonise. For example, decarbonising steel production involves switching from coal to gas.

The bills do include demand calibration to ensure gas prices are lower but do not sink to levels that would undermine, in particular, the economics of renewable energy and energy storage products or further undermine investment in other projects. Additionally, renewable gases and demand reduction will be able to be used to equip domestic supply obligations under the reservation. Together, these features ensure affordable, secure gas supply is achieved in a way consistent with our net zero and renewable energy ambitions.
The member's amendment also proposes limiting export licences to a maximum of 10 years.

It's important to our economy and to our country's future that Australia does remain a reliable trade and investment partner, so, in designing our domestic gas reservation scheme, the government has sought to balance protecting domestic supply while maintaining investment certainty and supply to nations that absolutely depend upon our country's energy exports for their long-term energy security. The long-term export licences within the regime provide the long-term regulatory certainty that is key to attracting investment to this country and to ensuring we have a energy-secure region. For these reasons, while I appreciate the input, the government will not be supporting the amendment.

Ms BOELE (Bradfield) (13:06): I rise to speak to the amendments circulated in my name to the Domestic Gas Reservation Bill 2026. In my second reading speech, I said that this bill is a step forward but that it leaves too much to ministerial discretion. These amendments deal with one of those discretions. Clause 27 lets the minister make an adjustment to an exporter's obligation to supply gas domestically under the reservation scheme. That means lowering or deferring the obligation. As drafted, the minister can do that in three ways: if the exporter can't reasonably supply enough gas to the domestic market because, for instance, of existing contracts, if it's already supplying gas under an existing reservation scheme like in WA, or if infrastructure constraints stand in the way. On their face, those are reasonable grounds, but the bill already recognises that there's more than one way to meet a domestic supply obligation. Under clause 19, the Gas Market Code can count things as domestic supply even though they aren't a direct gas sale—supplying renewable gas, reducing a gas exporters own gas use or helping other energy users cut their gas use, including through electrification.

I welcome this deemed supply provision because it recognises that the cheapest gas is the gas Australians never have to buy. The problem is that, in clause 27, the minister's discretion to adjust gas supply obligations ignores this part of the bill. An exporter could say, 'We can't get the molecules to market,' and have its domestic supply obligation reduced without the minister interrogating whether it could have met that obligation another way. My amendment seeks to strengthen the domestic supply obligation by ensuring that the minister can't make an adjustment unless the exporter is unable reasonably to meet its obligation through renewable gas or demand reduction. Before we let an exporter off the hook, we should check whether it could have helped a household switch to a heat pump or helped a factory electrify its process heat.

These amendments make the 'deemed DSO' component of the bill consistent with the 'DSO adjustment' part of the bill, and they ensure that, before companies are given a leave pass, they should try the cleaner options offered by electrification. Every adjustment to an exporter's domestic gas supply obligation is gas Australian households and businesses don't receive. So, if an exporter can still meet its obligation by lowering demand, the domestic market gets the same benefit, and a more enduring one, that lowers the cost of living, improves energy security and reduces emissions. While a gas reservation scheme might protect Australians from international gas prices, electrification means that they don't rely on that gas anymore. I commend the amendment to the House.

Ms MADELEINE KING (Brand—Minister for Resources and Minister for Northern Australia) (13:09): I thank the member for Bradfield for her engagement with respect to this package of domestic gas reservation bills. I understand the intent of the amendments proposed, and I agree with the member for Bradfield that there should be a very high bar when considering whether a domestic supply obligation should be varied. Variations for pre-existing contracts or infrastructure constraints should not be blanket exemptions—and, indeed, they absolutely are not. Additionally, there are disincentives in the scheme for seeking a domestic supply obligation variation, such as that exporters will not get the benefit of demand calibration where they already have a variation in place. Under the scheme, all exporters will be expected to make contributions to the domestic market commensurate with their export volumes. There are transitional provisions that protect existing commercial arrangements—that is, contracts executed before the scheme was announced on 22 December 2025—and that recognise that infrastructure constraints will take time to address. These provisions are transitional. Applications for variation are open only in the first year of the scheme.

As the responsible minister for each application I receive seeking a variation for a pre-existing contract, I will consider whether the full domestic supply obligation would cause the contract to be breached and whether there are practical alternatives to avoid a contract breach, such as bringing on additional supply or swaps. This ensures that supply obligations are met, including through demand reduction and renewable gas supply. Enabling more renewable gas supply is a really important part of this package, and I look forward to that. We absolutely support electrification. This government has invested heavily in batteries and solar panels for people's houses right around the county, and it's a really important initiative and part of our commitment to reaching net zero. This collection of bills, and the Domestic Gas Reservation Bill 2026 in particular, is a package around ensuring that Australians get benefit from the gas that belongs to this country and, in doing so, lowering prices and avoiding shortfalls into the future. So whilst I appreciate the amendments and the intent behind them, the government will not be supporting these amendments at this time.

Mrs PHILLIPS (Gilmore) (13:18): On behalf of the Joint Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs and Trade, I present the committee's report entitled Strengthening Australia's trade and investment relations with the countries of Africa.
Report made a parliamentary paper in accordance with standing order 39(e).

Mrs PHILLIPS: by leave—I'm pleased to present to the House this report. Africa is undergoing a dynamic economic transformation. It is home to some of the world's fastest growing economies; a rapidly expanding population, particularly its youth population; increasing urbanisation; and a growing middle class. The African continent represents one of the most significant opportunities for Australia's trade and investment agenda. At a time of growing geopolitical uncertainty and shifting global supply chains, expanding engagement with African economies offers Australia an opportunity to strengthen existing relations and develop trusted new partnerships. However, despite our longstanding cooperation and diplomatic relationships, the committee found that Australia's economic engagement with Africa remains well below potential. The inquiry examined the current nature of Australia's trade and investment relationship with Africa. While Australia has maintained a substantial presence in the resources sector across many African countries and has developed valuable commercial partnerships over several decades, total trade and investment flows remain modest when compared with the scale and diversity of opportunities available.

The committee heard that Australian businesses often confront a range of barriers when seeking to enter or expand within African markets. These include perceptions of sovereign and commercial risk, regulatory complexity, logistical challenges and insufficient access to market intelligence and in-country diplomatic and trade support. We heard that many Australian businesses remain unfamiliar with the considerable economic diversity that exists across Africa's 54 nations. Importantly, the evidence demonstrated that Africa should not be viewed as a single market. Rather, it is a continent comprised of diverse economies at varying stages of development, each offering distinct opportunities for trade, investment and commercial partnerships. The committee was particularly encouraged by evidence regarding opportunities for Australian exporters to diversify beyond traditional sectors. Australian expertise is increasingly sought after in critical minerals, renewable energy, agribusiness, education and training, digital technologies, health care and infrastructure development. As African economies industrialise and modernise, demand for Australian expertise and skills is likely to grow significantly.

The inquiry also considered the role of the African Continental Free Trade Area. When fully implemented, the African Continental Free Trade Area will create one of the world's largest free trade areas, supporting greater economic integration, reducing trade barriers and facilitating more efficient regional supply chains. The committee heard consistent evidence that the African Continental Free Trade Area has the potential to make African markets more accessible, predictable and attractive for Australian businesses. Australia's memorandum of understanding with the African Continental Free Trade Area provides substantial opportunity for collaboration, particularly Australia's expertise in regulatory and technical standards, but we must engage early.

The committee found that realising opportunities for diversification will require more focused engagement from the Australian government. Success in African markets demands long-term commitment, strong relationships, informed risk assessment and coordinated government support mechanisms. A recurring theme throughout the inquiry was the critical role that government can play in unlocking opportunities and reducing trade and investment barriers. The committee heard support for strengthened trade promotion, enhanced market intelligence, greater diplomatic and trade representation and improved coordination between government agencies, industry, the Australian African diaspora and the tertiary and vocational training sectors.

This report presents a series of recommendations aimed at strengthening Australia's economic engagement with Africa. These recommendations seek to provide a road map to improve Australia's trade architecture, increase commercial awareness, support export diversification and strengthen investment partnerships. At its core, this report is about partnerships—partnerships that support diversification, resilience and future prosperity. As global economic conditions continue to evolve, Australia must broaden its trade and investment agenda. Africa presents not only a significant economic opportunity but also an opportunity to deepen partnerships with a region that will play an increasingly important role in the global economy throughout the 21st century. The committee believes that, with strategic Australian government engagement and a focused long-term vision, Australia can develop a more ambitious and mutually beneficial economic relationship with the countries of Africa.

On behalf of the committee, I thank all those who contributed to this inquiry, including Australian exporters and investors, industry groups, academics and government agencies. Thank you also to African diplomatic representatives and members of Australia's African diaspora community. Their evidence provided valuable insights into both the opportunities and challenges shaping Australia's economic engagement with the African continent. I thank my fellow committee members for their constructive and collegiate engagement throughout the inquiry and commend this report to the House. I move:
That the House take note of the report.

Ms SPENDER (Wentworth) (13:30): I make this statement on behalf of the member for Indi, Dr Helen Haines, to continue her work. She has been a tireless advocate for equitable access to health care, regardless of where Australians live. Regional communities face critical shortages of GPs, specialists and allied-health professionals. Families are travelling hundreds of kilometres for essential treatment, facing long waiting lists and paying significant out-of-pocket costs. The member for Indi previously called our attention to the $9.23 billion annual health spending gap between metropolitan and regional and rural Australia. Where you live should not determine the quality of health care you receive, but there's no single fix. We need a coordinated approach that improves access and affordability, and injecting more spending in health is where it starts. The member for Indi has proposed a $2 billion building regional and rural hospital fund, a fully costed plan to help regional hospitals replace ageing infrastructure and plan for the future. In the member for Indi's words, regional Australians aren't asking for special treatment, just the same access to health care as everyone else. Today we stand together to carry that work forward. On behalf of the community of Warringah, I would like to join my community to the community of Indi in putting this request to the government.
Environmental Conservation

Mr DREYFUS (Isaacs) (13:31): I rise today to recognise the talented students from my electorate of Isaacs, whose artwork was shared with me by the Australian Conservation Foundation as part of the Wild At Art threatened species competition. I am really impressed by their creativity and their passion about the need to protect Australia's unique wildlife. Their paintings and drawings are a wonderful reminder of the important role young people can play in these conservation efforts. Australia's environment, from our coastlines to waterways and bushland, need to be protected, and climate change is a major threat to our native species. The Australian government is committed to preventing further extinctions and recovering endangered wildlife. We've protected an extra 95 million hectares of land and ocean. More than half of Australia's ocean waters are now protected. To the students who entered the competition: your artwork shows that you care deeply about our wildlife and its future. I encourage you to turn that passion into action. There are many groups you can volunteer with who care about nature and work together to protect it. You could contact Junior Landcare with a parent or carer to ask about ways to get involved. Your family and friends will be proud to see you using your creativity to speak up for a cause that you believe in. I certainly am.
Defence

Mr JOYCE (New England) (13:33): I rise today in support of Australia's veterans, returned servicemen and -women, and ex-service men and women. There are three issues I think that need to be discussed clearly. First was the debacle, which was the $5,000 allied health issue. I have no idea why that cap was there. It was a bad policy when it came in. It didn't last. It was put aside. It should never have happened. The second thing is what on earth is going on with Victoria Barracks? How can you come into one of the icons of Australia and—I don't know what you intend to do with it—turn it into a theme park? Do we realise how pertinent that is to the defence of our nation and to the iconography of Sydney that it sees its attachments to the Defence Force? It's somewhere I believe even my grandfather, who was in artillery and came over here from New Zealand, spent some time with as a servicemen. It means so much to Australia. It's an absurdity.

The final thing is the so-called Frontier Wars, the wars of Australians against Australians. This should not be in the Australian War Memorial. This is an outrage. The Australian War Memorial is for Australians who served overseas and domestically in protection of Australia, not in some sort of domestic issue. No-one in an Australian uniform was ever directed by an Australian officer to serve in that conflict. Just don't do this to us.
Prime Minister's Spelling Bee

Ms URQUHART (Braddon) (13:34): Pusillanimous is a word that is not easy to say, let alone spell. But not for 13-year-old Charlotte Edwards from Braddon—in fact, from my home town—who entered the Prime Minister's Spelling Bee competition and went on to win the years 7 and 8 spelling category. She's the first ever national winner from Tasmania. Charlotte travelled to Canberra with her mum, Anna; her dad, Shaun; and little sister Lexie on Monday this week. The competition is in its sixth year, and it received a record 90,000 entries. This year, for the first time, the wins in all three categories were taken out by girls.

Charlotte attends Leighland Christian School in Ulverstone, where I'm sure they're all bragging about having the first ever national winner of the competition as a student of their lovely school. Charlotte brought along her dictionary, which she asked the Prime Minister to sign. I was there while he signed it, and she said to me:
It was very exciting but I was nervous because he is the Prime Minister of the entire country.

So I want to thank our prime minister for taking that time to sign Charlotte's dictionary, because I know it meant a lot to her. Charlotte said that, when she told her friends that she was coming to parliament, they were all pretty proud of her for getting so far in the competition. We are also very proud of you, Charlotte. Well done to you and good luck for your schooling future.
Bradfield Youth Forum

Ms BOELE (Bradfield) (13:36): I want to recognise and thank the inaugural members of the Bradfield Youth Forum, a group that I established because a young constituent wrote to me, twice in fact, asking how young people in our community could share their perspectives and contribute meaningfully to local and national conversations. My sincere thanks goes to the 13 students who have given their time, their energy and their ideas and to their schools, Roseville College, St Ives High School, Glenaeon Rudolf Steiner School, Turramurra High School, Northern Beaches Secondary College, Knox Grammar School and Abbotsleigh.

This group has met several times, and they've chosen three priorities: the financial pressures on young people, particularly housing and HECS; transparency in government spending; and education funding and equity. But they weren't content just to identify problems. They researched and tested their ideas, and their final proposal is what I've called the 'Bradfield budget challenge', a competition that invites local students to imagine themselves as the Treasurer and build their own federal budget. The Bradfield budget challenge will allow young people to understand where public money goes and make the case for change. These inspirational young people may not be able to vote yet, but they have all the knowledge and the skills and the grit, frankly, that they absolutely need to make sure that they have a say in the decisions that they make here. On behalf of Bradfield, I'd like to congratulate them.
World Teachers' Day

Mr SOON (Banks) (13:37): Tomorrow, 30 October, is World Teacher's Day here in Australia, and I want to take this opportunity to thank all of the incredible teachers and educators across my electorate of Banks, and indeed all across our great country, for the incredible work that they do. It's the early childhood teachers and educators, including more than 700 in my electorate of Banks, who are benefiting from this government's decision to fund a historic pay rise, meaning their skills and work are reflected not just in rhetoric but in their pay packets as well. It's the teachers in primary and secondary schools who are getting the resources they need as a result of this government's decision to put every single public school on the path to full funding. And it's the vocational education teachers at our TAFEs, whose students are able to get qualified without the burden of student debt as a result of fee-free TAFE. I say to all of the teachers across my electorate of Banks and all across this country: you do incredible work and at times very difficult and challenging work educating our next generation. We sincerely, from the bottom of our hearts, thank you for it.
Nuclear Energy

Mr BOYCE (Flynn) (13:39): Imagine a clean energy system so small it fits in the back of a ute but powerful enough to run nearly a thousand homes continuously for a whole five years without using a drop of water. That is the modern nuclear microreactor. An Australian team has actually built one in America in just over 155 days, proving how fast and safe and easy it is to move this technology and what it's become.

Our world and technology are changing rapidly. AI is booming and massive computer data centres need more power non-stop, 24 hours a day, seven days a week. While solar panels and wind turbines produce so-called green energy, computers, hospitals and factories cannot simply stop working when the sun sets or the wind drops. Around the world, companies already use these mini-nuclear generators to power data centres, remote mines and towns cheaply without polluting the air. Yet right here in Australia, old federal laws made decades ago keep this clean energy technology banned in Australia. It is time to update our laws by lifting the nuclear moratorium. We can power our digital future, lower our electricity bills, protect our environment and let Australian innovators build a cleaner, stronger energy system right here in Australia.
Brain Cancer

Ms COFFEY (Griffith) (13:40): A fortnight ago I attended Brain Tumour Alliance Australia's Head to the Hill event here at Parliament House. It was a deeply moving reminder of the devastating impact this disease has on Australian families. I want to share the words of Jessica, from Greenslopes in my community, whose eight-year-old son Max underwent brain surgery recently:
A few months ago, Max was an ordinary eight-year-old boy, playing cricket and soccer, building in Minecraft and laughing with his friends at school.
Then an MRI we thought was checking for concussion revealed something no parent ever expects to hear; our son had a brain tumour.
Within weeks, Max underwent almost nine hours of brain surgery.
It saved his life, but his life is changed forever.
We are incredibly grateful that Max survived, but not every family gets that outcome.
Brain cancer has a five-year survival rate of only around 23 percent and remains the leading cause of cancer death in Australian children and adults under 40.
Australia has world-class doctors, scientists and researchers.
What we need is the investment to give them a better chance of changing these numbers.
I thank Jessica for sharing Max's story and also thank Pam Hubner for her tireless advocacy in memory of her daughter Angie.

The Albanese government has invested close to $20 million through the Medical Research Future Fund in childhood brain cancer research, supporting new treatments and a national clinical trial. We've also made a further $8.4 million available for brain cancer research and new therapies. We must continue investing in our research as there's more work to do to give people who have brain cancer more hope.
Economy

Ms PENFOLD (Lyne) (13:42): Yesterday the Treasurer stood at the dispatch box and tried to blame Australia's inflation crisis on a war overseas. But yesterday the Reserve Bank governor, Michele Bullock, told Australians something very different:
Importantly though, it is not just these global pressures that are driving inflation in Australia.

She warned of persistent domestic inflationary pressures, weak productivity and demand exceeding our economy's capacity to supply—and she confirmed that government spending contributes to that demand. Yet the Treasurer wants Australians to believe this crisis is everyone else's fault but his own.

Inflation has risen to 4.3 per cent. The Foodbank hunger report tells us that one in three Australian households is experiencing food insecurity. Families are going hungry while this Treasurer plays politics with the truth. If Jim Chalmers cannot be honest with himself about—

The DEPUTY SPEAKER

Ms PENFOLD: If the Treasurer cannot be honest with himself about the causes of inflation, how can he be honest with the Australian people? Australians are paying the price at the supermarket checkout, in their mortgage repayments and in the meals they can no longer afford. Australians deserve a Treasurer who takes responsibility, not one who twists the warnings of the Reserve Bank to suit his political narrative. Stop the excuses. Stop the blame-shifting. Take responsibility, because Australians cannot afford another four years of Labor's economic failures.
Bonnici, Mr Mark

Dr REID (Robertson) (13:43): Today I rise to acknowledge Mr Mark Bonnici, who will retire as principal of St Edward's College in East Gosford at the end of the school year. Mr Bonnici has led St Edward's for almost a decade, but his service to the college began long before that. As a PE teacher, he taught young men about their physical health and mental health, and the importance of looking after both. As a doctor, I can tell the House that so much of a person's health is shaped long before they ever sit in a GP's surgery, and teachers like Mr Bonnici play a big part in that.

As a principal, Mr Bonnici placed social justice at the heart of the college. Under his leadership, St Edward's has stepped up its fundraising for disadvantaged communities in Kenya and its support for local organisations helping people doing it tough on the Central Coast. Leading a school is not just about the students in front of you; it is about an entire community of young people, their families and their staff who serve them. Over his career, Mr Bonnici has shaped the lives of thousands of young men, giving them quality education and a commitment to justice, to peace and to standing up for those who are less fortunate. Mr Bonnici, on behalf of the people of the Central Coast, thank you for your dedication, your leadership and indeed your service, and I wish you a long, happy and a well-earned retirement.
Economy

Today is a very significant day for Australia's energy security. Today, the first Australian national gas reservation scheme passed through this chamber. This is a landmark reform of this Albanese Labor government. The Albanese Labor government is getting on with the job of securing more Australian gas for Australian households, businesses and manufacturers. Australia has abundant gas resources and Australians should benefit from them. Australian households and industry should have access to the gas they need at affordable prices. That means reliable and plentiful energy for households, certainty for manufacturers and industry, and support for Australian jobs and investment. At its heart, this national gas reservation scheme is about making sure Australian gas delivers for Australians.

There are some steps remaining in delivering this scheme. When it goes to the other place, every single senator in that place will have the opportunity to support our landmark legislation establishing a long-term and enduring domestic gas reservation scheme, under which LNG exporters will be required to make a genuine contribution to the Australian market through a domestic supply obligation. It will be linked to their export volumes. The obligation will be flexible, with the Australian Energy Regulator able to calibrate the obligation to reflect the domestic demand, supply and market conditions. More gas available to Australian customers means a better supplied domestic market and downward pressure on prices.

I want to thank all the MPs in this chamber for their constructive engagement on this important reform. The problem of gas supply in this country has been recognised for some time and it has taken some time for a government to step up and take up the responsibility to fix it. And that is what this government is doing. This is a Labor government that gets things done. This is a Labor government that delivers and delivers for the Australian people. For years and years, across multiple governments and many parliaments, a national gas reservation scheme has been too hard—a bridge too far. But we have taken up the challenge. We have done the hard work and produced a gas reservation scheme that will deliver Australian gas for Australian people.

This is Australian gas and it should be available to Aussies first, whether it's Australian households or Australian industry—Australian resources working for Australians. Mr BURKE (Watson—Minister for the Arts, Minister for Home Affairs, Minister for Cyber Security, Minister for Immigration and Citizenship and Leader of the House) (14:33): I thank the member for Reid in raising issues that were honoured last night when the Police Federation of Australia held this year's National Police Bravery Awards, where we acknowledge the work not only of the Australian Federal Police but of all those who form the police services and police forces around the states and territories. Mr BURKE: The National Police Bravery Award is an award by police for police. Last night, there were two different groups—one individual and one group of officers—who were honoured. The group that was honoured, who were represented last night by Andy Williams from the Queensland police force, were those officers who responded to the Wieambilla shooting. In December 2022 four police officers arrived and, without warning, were shot at. While doing their jobs Matthew Arnold and Rachel McCrow were murdered. After the initial barrage of fire, Constable Keely Brough and Constable Randall Kirk found cover in nearby bushland at separate locations. Child Safety
Mr SOON (Banks) (14:59): My question is to the Attorney-General. How is the Albanese government leading work with the states and territories to keep our children and young people safe?

Ms ROWLAND (Greenway—Attorney-General) (15:00): I thank the member for his question. I want to acknowledge that tomorrow is Day for Daniel, Australia's largest national event dedicated to child safety, education and awareness. Child sexual abuse is an abhorrent crime, and perpetrators must face the full force of the law, because one instance of child sexual abuse is one too many, and we must do everything we can to prevent this from occurring.

In August, I updated the House on our progress with the states and territories on working with children checks, and it follows the Commonwealth's delivery of these reforms through the Standing Council of Attorneys-General. 'Banned in one, banned in all' is now law in every Australian jurisdiction. It means that a person prohibited from working with children in one part of Australia cannot simply cross a border and seek a clearance somewhere else. That is real practical reform, closing gaps between systems that could otherwise put children at risk.

The evidence shows that our reforms are working. In Victoria, exclusions from working with children checks have increased from 965 in 2023-24 to 1,762 in 2025-26. Just let that sink in. The number of working with children checks refused has almost doubled between that reporting period. Victorian authorities have also used strengthened powers to immediately suspend or ban 118 people based on serious safety concerns and intelligence received from police and regulators. These are exactly the kinds of reforms that the royal commission into child sexual abuse envisaged—earlier identification of risk, stronger information sharing and proactive intervention before children are harmed. Recent reporting on the extradition of Ashley Paul Griffith, known as Australia's worst paedophile, highlights why these reforms matter. Where historical allegations, regulatory information or interstate concerns exist, stronger information sharing and nationally consistent risk assessments improve our ability to take action early. I also welcome Queensland's reforms to implement the nationally consistent baseline standards and exclusion criteria agreed by SCAG.

These advances are supported by federal funding, the Albanese government's $37 million national continuous checking capability, which enables near-real-time monitoring of criminal history and represents significant progress towards a national system that better protects children and young people. There is more to do, but we will keep working every day to deliver real change that keeps our children safe.
