p.span: Moncrieff Electorate: Community Events
Tourism Industry
Migration

Ms BELL (Moncrieff) (16:40): I recently had the privilege of joining Zonta Gold Coast Inc for its inaugural event, themed 'Celebrate, Connect and Change'. It was a fantastic evening, where we marked a new chapter for Zonta on the Gold Coast, while honouring almost three decades of outstanding service by Zonta Paradise Point. Zonta's commitment to advancing the status of women and girls through service and advocacy is truly commendable. I was honoured to join the event panel alongside the exceptional Lucy Gregory, CEO of the Domestic Violence Prevention Centre; and inspirational young students from Benowa State High School and the Queensland Academies Health Sciences Campus. The evening highlighted the importance of celebrating women's achievements, building meaningful connections and partnerships, and driving the change needed to ensure every girl has the opportunity to thrive. I thank the dedicated team of Zonta Gold Coast for their important work in our community and give a particular shout out to Kathryn Janovsky, who is a member of my Moncrieff Community Cabinet, doing great work across the Gold Coast.

I also recently had the pleasure of joining the Little Grubbs Orchard Foundation in my electorate for its community fundraiser and trivia night at the Sofitel Gold Coast Broadbeach. The foundation raises critical funds to provide assistance, therapy, education and essential allied-health support for children with autism, disability or special needs. These funds help families cover costs not met by the NDIS, ensuring that children can access the vital support they need. I give a huge thank you to the founder, Lily Grubb, and her children for their incredible work to support our community's most vulnerable.

Earlier this month, I was proud to welcome the Leader of the Nationals and shadow minister for trade, investment and tourism, Senator Matt Canavan, to my electorate on the Gold Coast. Tourism is one of the biggest drivers of our local economy, contributing $8.6 billion in the last financial year alone. As one of Australia's leading tourism destinations, our city depends on a strong, reliable workforce to welcome visitors, support local businesses and keep our economy moving. During Senator Canavan's visit, we met with some of the Gold Coast leading tourism operators to hear first hand about the impact of Labor's changes to the Working Holiday Maker visa program. We spoke with Dylan Hunt from the SkyPoint Observation Deck and met with key industry stakeholders including Anthony Ardern from the Tour Collective Group, John Warn and Rachel Hancock from Experience Gold Coast, the Hon. Will Hodgman AC from Invest Gold Coast and Clark Kirby from Village Roadshow. These people understand our tourism industry better than anyone, and they are deeply concerned about the consequences of this government's decisions. Tourism businesses rely on seasonal workers to meet demand during peak holiday periods—there's no doubt—and, without enough staff, businesses cannot operate at full capacity, visitors miss out, revenue suffers, and opportunities to create local jobs are lost. At a time when small businesses are already battling rising costs and economic uncertainty, the last thing they need is a government making it harder to access the workers they depend on. Labor's changes to working holiday visas have created further uncertainty for an industry that needs certainty to plan, invest and grow.

Migration must work for Australia. It should fill critical skills gaps, strengthen our economy and support our communities, not place unnecessary pressure on businesses that are already doing it tough. That is why the coalition has announced its Australia-first migration plan. We must recognise that migration numbers need to come down, but it must be done in a considered way that puts Australia's needs first. Our plan will reduce net overseas migration to 100,000 a year for the first two years, while protecting critical regional workforce programs, including those supporting tourism and hospitality. It will prioritise skilled migration, improve the skills mix of arrivals and ensure our migration system better serves our national interest, because getting migration right is not simply about reducing numbers; it's about making sure our country has the right skills in the right places.

The Gold Coast tourism industry is vital to our local jobs, our small businesses and our economic future. This government should be listening to the people on the ground who understand what our industry needs, rather than imposing changes that risk undermining its success. The coalition will back our tourism operators, protect the workers our industries need and restore a migration system that works for Australia. Our tourism businesses deserve nothing less.
Hunter Electorate: Mining Industry

Mr REPACHOLI (Hunter) (16:45): I want to talk about something that's incredibly important to the Hunter: jobs. We need good, secure, well-paid jobs that allow families to put food on the table, pay their mortgages and build their futures in the communities that they call home, and that's why the recent approval of the Hunter Valley Operations continuation project is such a significant win for our region. This isn't about opening a brand new coal mine. It's about allowing an existing operation to continue supporting the workers, businesses and communities that rely on it and it's about recognising the enormous contribution mining continues to make to the Hunter and to this beautiful country, Australia.

HVO supports around 1,500 mine workers and has relationships with approximately 750 suppliers. Over four years it contributed an estimated $6.9 billion to our economy. That's an enormous contribution and one that deserves recognition in this parliament. Behind those figures are real people: the miners heading off to work before sunrise; the fitters, the leccos, the boilies, the operators and the apprentices; the small businesses supplying parts, equipment and services; and the local shops, sporting clubs and community organisations that benefit when those workers spend their wages locally. Mining doesn't just support the people working behind the mine gates; it supports entire communities.

I'm a former coal miner myself. I know what these jobs mean for families because I've worked alongside the people doing them, and I'm tired of hearing mining workers being spoken about as if they're somehow part of the problem. They are not. They are hardworking Aussies who have helped build this country and will continue playing an important role in its future.

Now let's talk about the environment, because I believe we can support our mining industry and take climate change seriously also. Australia has committed to reaching net zero emissions by 2050, but what does net zero actually mean? It doesn't mean producing absolutely no emissions. It means reducing greenhouse gas emissions as far as possible and balancing the remaining emissions out through genuine removal from the atmosphere. Every time we fart, we produce methane. Every time we breathe, we produce carbon dioxide. That's part of the natural carbon cycle, and it's different from releasing additional carbon into the atmosphere from burning fossil fuels.

The challenge is reducing the additional emissions driving climate change, and that means looking at the full picture. Solar panels don't magically appear in paddocks. Wind turbines don't just grow out of the ground. Electric vehicles don't arrive at dealerships without someone mining the materials, manufacturing the components and transporting them right around the world. All of that requires energy, resources and industrial activity. All of that has an environmental footprint. Over their operating lives, renewable energy and electric vehicles can deliver substantial emissions savings that outweigh much of the initial impact, and that's why they're part of the solution, but we can't pretend the environmental costs of building them don't exist. We need to measure emissions properly across the whole lifecycle and apply consistent standards. You can't demand an honest accounting of coal's environmental impacts while ignoring the mining and manufacturing needed for technologies replacing it.

There's also an important conversation to be had about the quality of coal being used around the world. Some Australian coal has advantages over lower-quality alternatives, including higher energy content and lower impurities. That can improve efficiency and reduce certain pollutants, but emissions depend on the coal, the power station and how it's used. We should be making decisions based on evidence, not slogans. While countries continue to use coal, Australia has an opportunity to supply customers under strong environmental and workplace and safety standards. The world is changing and our region is changing with it, but transition won't happen overnight. We cannot expect regional communities to carry the entire burden while everyone else enjoys the benefits of the energy, steel and resources they produce.

The Hunter has powered this country for generations and the skills of our miners, our engineers, our tradies and our manufacturers will help build the next generation of energy infrastructure too. The minerals, machinery, steel and expertise needed for the transition all have to come from somewhere. Mining will be part of this and how we reach net zero also. So let's support our workers, back responsible mining and invest in the industries of tomorrow. The Hunter deserves a future with both a strong economy and a healthier environment.

To every miner out there, thank you for what you do. You go into very dangerous environments every day of the week. Keep up the great work. While people want to buy our coal, we'll always sell them our coal. So, to the miners in the Hunter, remember, we have your backs. We'll support you along the way. Thank you for what you do. Cheers!
Mitchell Youth Leadership Forum

Mr HAWKE (Mitchell) (16:50): This year marks 25 years of the Mitchell Youth Leadership Forum, a singularly successful program in Australia bringing together every public and private high school in my electorate and some from outside my electorate. There are 300 children every year who come and learn about three core values: service, integrity and courage. The Mitchell Youth Leadership Forum has, over those 25 years, had an impact on literally tens of thousands of young people.

All of the kids who come along get put into small groups. They don't know a single person in them. Each group has leaders, one man and one woman, who are former students and have been trained in leadership—young people leading young people. Over three days, without their phones, they immerse themselves with people they don't know in leadership exercises based on the themes of those three values and hear from great speakers. This year, we heard from Lucinda Harvey on breaking barriers and building community; Bianca Kulikovskis on courage to create; Chris Lee on leading yourself; Akanisi Ledua on leading with service and inspiring with purpose; and Josh and Nathan Katz on whatever it takes. Over the years, we've had Young Australians of the Year and some singularly impressive Australians come and speak.

I want to give a shout out this year in particular to Her Excellency the Governor-General, Sam Mostyn, who came and addressed and spoke with the 250 young people who were gathered in their teams, after their community services component. This year, community service involved dealing with projects at Aminya Village, McCall Gardens, Riding for the Disabled and Tall Timbers Centre—great community institutions at which the children learned about serving others.

Her Excellency was outstanding in her presentation. Those young people had an opportunity to engage with the woman at the apex of our constitution, at the apex of constitutional power, and to simply ask her about her leadership journey, her commitment to service and her constitutional role. I want to thank Her Excellency for being there in Castle Hill. Everyone was in Castle Hill on that day, it seems. The Premier was there, and the Deputy Premier was there. Her Excellency made the time to come and enthusiastically visit 300 young leaders, and it was an excellent exchange. They will remember that for life. I praise the person that she is and her great spirit that led her to her role and her commitment to leaders and young leadership in Australia.

I want to take time to thank the committee. This annual event, three days with these kids, is a year-long endeavour. We had great sponsors of the forum this year: Nature's Sunshine Products of Australia, Castle Towers, QIC and Peppers The Hills Lodge. Their dedication and their financial commitment enable these young leaders to come together, engage, get to know each other and strengthen the fabric of my north-western community, with kids who never knew each other leaving with friendships for life. The committee that runs it comprises Tristan Smith, Ronie Quinn, Steve Edwards, Jan Cox, Ged Lewis, Thomas Kelly, Jessie Peake, Ken Shaw, Daniel Ridley, Marcus Cannon, Jane Porto, Lauren Nowacka, Chloe Lahood, Ronan Pillay, Deyyan Jafar and Simon Teh, most of whom are now on the board after 25 years and are former students who have been through the program themselves. Their voluntary commitment year round is just absolutely amazing. I also want to thank the CEO, Tristan Smith. He's a young teacher who works with the Department of Education. He's a former student as well. He came out of Kellyville High School, and he's now with the Department of Education. He's an outstanding man. His leadership was something to behold at this forum. The challenge we had this year was that our regular site on the banks of the Nepean River is being refitted, so we were at Katoomba, at StayKCC. I want to thank StayKCC also for their outstanding commitment. A three-day program with this many kids and involving this much commitment, time and effort—and with all of the community work, the challenges and the other things that go with it, day and night—couldn't be done without this impressive team.

After 25 years, and having served as either the chair or the patron for 17 years myself, I can't speak highly enough to members of parliament of getting youth together, hearing from them and letting them immerse themselves, without their digital devices, in the simple principles of service, integrity and courage around some excellent Australians. It produces great results.

I thank everybody who's given us so much over 25 years. I thank my predecessor, Alan Cadman, for founding this forum. We've modernised it. We've expanded it. We get schools from Indigenous Australia. We do everything we can to make it available to everybody. It's a special thing. I particularly pay tribute to Her Excellency the Governor-General for taking a moment of her time to do something very special for these young Australians.
Krishnan, Dr Easwaran

Dr REID (Robertson) (16:55): Every nation tells a story about itself, and tonight I want to tell a quieter part of ours. It belongs to a man who spent his life at the front gates of the hospital. His name is Dr Easwaran Krishnan, and after 48 years of service to medicine he is handing over for the last time. His journey began in Delhi. He trained at the Armed Forces Medical College and wore the uniform of the Indian Air Force. Medicine then carried him across the world to the United Arab Emirates, to the United Kingdom and then, finally, to us. He could have gone anywhere but he chose Australia, and he spent the best years of his life keeping our people alive.

Let's think about what that means. When a young man was pulled from a car on a dark freeway and brought to hospital, Dr Krishnan was there. When a mother ran through the sliding doors at three in the morning, holding a child who was not breathing, searching for anyone that knew what to do, he was there. Night after night, year after year, Christmas mornings, missed birthdays, long drives home at dawn—he bore it all, quietly, so the rest of us could sleep. There are Australians at their kitchen tables tonight because of Dr Krishnan—fathers who walked their daughters down the aisle, children who grew up never knowing how close they came.

His name is written in the stories of many, including my own. He was my very first supervising emergency physician, and I can still recall to this very day his calm instruction. In an emergency department that is so often built for speed, he always found the time to be gentle. He taught me that truth is a kindness, even when it breaks your heart to say it. He taught me that the cleaner and the professor deserve the same respect. And he taught me that integrity is what you do at four o'clock in the morning when you are exhausted, when you are tired, when no-one is watching, and the only witness to that interaction is your own conscience. He is part of the reason I became an emergency doctor and he is part of the reason that I stand here in this chamber tonight.

And I am one of many; there are many people right across this nation and right around the world—the many doctors, the many nurses, allied health professionals and other health staff—who carry him right into every shift. Every steady hand, every hard truth told gently and every life pulled back from the edge, Dr Krishnan is there. That is a legacy. It's not marble, it's not monuments—it's people. Australia is the sum of the people who give themselves to it, and Dr Krishnan has given us everything. I say to his family: thank you for sharing him with us.

Dr Krishnan, for 48 years you stood at the front gates and you made sure that all those that came through the hospital—fathers, sons, mothers, daughters, friends, family and loved ones—were never ever alone. Tonight you hand over to us, and we stand ready for you. Dr Krishnan, on behalf of all those people right across the Central Coast and those who'll be listening at Wyong Hospital, thank you for everything you've done for us and thank you for everything you've done for our community. I wish you all the very best in your retirement, my friend.

CONSTITUENCY STATEMENTS
Thriving Kids Program
Ms BOELE (Bradfield) (09:53): On 30 September, I brought together parents, carers, disability providers.

p.span: Ms BOELE: On 30 September, I brought together parents, carers, disability advocates, allied health professionals, educators, service providers and New South Wales government representatives for a community roundtable on the new Thriving Kids program. I also invited members of the Bradfield community to share their thoughts and questions through a survey. I heard from 78 people—parents and carers but also health professionals, educators, service providers and community organisations—and 66 others submitted questions or comments to policymakers. I organised this event because, since Thriving Kids was announced, many, many people have contacted my office to share their thoughts and concerns about the changes. Thank you to everyone who participated, particularly those who shared deeply personal experiences about the challenges facing their children.

Everyone I heard from wants the same thing from Thriving Kids: for children to receive appropriate and effective support early so they have every opportunity to learn, participate and thrive. But the message from my community is also very clear that families and frontline professionals do not have enough information about how this major reform will operate. Parents fear that children could fall through the cracks between the NDIS and the new system. They're worried about losing trusted therapists, established relationships and supports tailored to their children's individual needs. Families and healthcare professionals alike questioned whether group based services will be suitable for children, particularly those with complex or co-occurring needs. They also raised important questions about privacy, choice and control safeguards, accountability and how children's individual needs will be assessed. There is a concern that programs will be rushed and implemented with inadequate data-gathering analysis. Allied health professionals and small-service providers told me that they're also facing considerable uncertainty. They don't know yet what role they'll have in the new system, how services will be commissioned or whether their businesses will even remain viable.

Thriving Kids must not simply shift responsibility from one overstretched system to the other. Nor should reform come at the cost of continuity of care or the trusted relationships that families have spent years building. Participants understood that a reform of this scale will involve some difficult implementation challenges, but they rightly expect governments to communicate changes clearly and well in advance and to work closely with families and frontline professionals. I'll keep listening to my community as Thriving Kids is rolled out. I will continue pressing for clear, timely communication, strong safeguards and accountability, proper workforce planning and genuine continuity of care. I'll push for the voices of children and families to be at the centre of reform. No family should be left to navigate this transition alone.
Migration

Mr GOSLING (Solomon) (10:07): The Albanese Labor government strongly supports a tailored and targeted migration system. We are making changes to the system to give us more control over who arrives, who stays and who leaves. I've been speaking with relevant ministerial colleagues about the concerns being raised by the tourism and agricultural sector in my electorate of Solomon—Darwin and Palmerston—around working holiday makers. I met recently with the MEC NT Electrical Contractors team. They, too, reinforced the importance of the working holiday maker cohort and the opportunity to tap into a skilled workforce who want to stay in the Territory longer. I've been speaking with some of our major hostels in Darwin—Deb from Youth Shack Backpackers and Stratton from MoM Darwin, a backpacker hostel on Mitchell Street—about the impact of the recently announced changes.

Similarly, a constituent wrote to me about their personal experience of arriving in Darwin from Ireland as a backpacker in 2011, planning to be working holiday maker. Like many, they intended to stay only a few weeks during the dry season before continuing their travels, but during that time they secured employment in the hospitality sector and were later offered employer sponsorship. That opportunity changed the course of their life and is the sole reason they are still living and thriving in Darwin today. Fifteen years later, they have built a career in the Territory, purchased their own home, started a family and are contributing extensively to community life through volunteer work.

Just last week, I got my hair cut at Diamond Barbers, who always do a great job, and my barber was—you guessed it, Deputy Speaker Sharkie—once a working holiday maker. I attended the 50th anniversary of Amity Community Services recently. Some of those counsellors had studied—
